name: Lydia Marchmont
languages: French (a governess's French, improved on a Mississippi steamboat)
equipment: A grey travelling dress with a bustle she says is for fashion and is mostly for pockets, and a velvet-collared coat
Derringer (Remington over-and-under, .41), 2 loaded, in a garter holster or a muff, depending on the company
Boot knife with a mother-of-pearl handle
Three decks of cards, one of them honest
A faro dealing box with a spring she can work with her little finger, which she keeps for teaching purposes
A share certificate: one-twentieth part of the Lodestar Mining Company of Argent, won from Aurelius Stannard at a poker table in May
A small ledger of every dividend the share has paid, all in cash, none in bullion
A pocket watch engraved to someone else, a silver flask of brandy and a box of Turkish cigarettes
A carpet bag with a second dress, a good pair of gloves and a Bible she has never opened, which is where she keeps her money
features: Book Learning (Back East origin: advantage on Investigation checks to read documents such as deeds, contracts, ledgers, share certificates and telegrams; once per long rest she recalls one useful fact about a law, a process, a science or a piece of history; bankers and lawyers treat her as one of their own)

Read the Table (Gambler: her proficiency bonus is doubled for Gambling and Insight checks; once per short or long rest, after a minute of watching or talking to someone, she learns one thing they are hiding, as a true sentence from the GM; she always knows whether a game is honest)

Ace in the Hole (Gambler: once per turn, extra damage to a creature she hits with a finesse Melee weapon or a Sidearm when she has advantage, an ally is beside the target, or the target believed her lie within the last minute; 2d6 at 3rd level; not part of the damage on her sheet)
Lady Luck (Gambler, 2nd level: luck points equal to her CHA modifier per long rest; spend one to roll an extra d20 on an attack, check or save, or to make an attacker reroll against her)

Sleeve Gun (Gambler, 2nd level: she draws a concealable weapon as a bonus action without anyone not watching her hands noticing, has advantage on Sleight of Hand to carry one past a search, and can Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action)

Game: Faro Dealer (Gambler, 3rd level: she can set up a faro bank in any town with a saloon and earn 1d6 x 5 dollars a night, and the house always knows who is winning, who is drinking and who is broke)
Know the Games (Card Sharp background: she knows every game played west of the Mississippi and every house that runs one, and can always find a game, a stake or a dealer who owes her a favor)

personality.traits: I quote odds on everything, including whether a man is lying. I am always polite. I never drink at the table and I always appear to.
personality.ideals: A fair game is the most honest thing in America. I cheat only cheats, and only when they have it coming.
personality.bonds: My twentieth share of the Lodestar, which is the first thing I have ever owned that I did not have to carry. And my younger brother Edmund's school fees in Philadelphia, which he thinks our father pays.
personality.flaws: I cannot walk away from a puzzle or a dare. And I despise rich men who think they are clever, which is most of them, and they can tell.

appearance: A tall, fair woman of thirty-one with a long elegant face, grey eyes that look amused at everything, and ash-blonde hair pinned up under a small hat with a grey feather. She dresses like a respectable widow from Philadelphia, which is how she started, and has hands like a pianist's that are never still.
backstory: Lydia Marchmont is the daughter of a Quaker bank clerk in Philadelphia who taught her arithmetic and probability as a game, and was horrified when she began beating his friends at whist for money. At nineteen she was a governess; at twenty-two she was dealing faro on a Mississippi steamboat, having discovered that the river paid a woman who could count cards far better than a family paid one who could teach French. She came west with the silver boom and has dealt at the Silver Dollar in Argent since March. In May, Aurelius Stannard, the camp's first citizen and the president of its Mining Association, lost a large hand to her and, laughing, paid with a one-twentieth share in his Lodestar mine. Since then the Lodestar has paid her four dividends, generous ones, always in cash, always in new Denver banknotes, never in bullion, though the Lodestar is supposed to be the richest mine in the basin. A share-owner may inspect the books. She has asked twice and been charmingly put off twice. On Saturday seventy of the Lodestar's silver bars, one-twentieth of them hers in law, go out on the first train. She has bought a ticket. She wants to see them.
